package_info.package_manager: N/A (custom malware, delivered via phishing or exploit)
package_info.why_malicious: PowerLess Backdoor is a custom PowerShell-based implant attributed to the Iranian APT35 group, designed for covert remote access and espionage. It evades detection by executing PowerShell code in-memory within a .NET application, avoiding the creation of a powershell.exe process, which is commonly monitored by security solutions. Its primary functions include persistent unauthorized remote control, command execution, and data exfiltration from compromised systems.

execution_context.trigger: post-compromise, upon execution of the malicious .NET payload
execution_context.file_location: Malicious .NET executable (location varies, often in user profile or temp directories)
required_permissions: filesystem (for reading/writing files and collecting data)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The .NET application loads and executes PowerShell scripts directly in memory using the System.Management.Automation namespace, without writing scripts to disk or spawning powershell.exe. The implant establishes an encrypted channel to a remote C2 server, receives and executes attacker-supplied PowerShell commands, and sends execution results and exfiltrated data back to the C2 server.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution of the malicious .NET payload, the application loads and runs PowerShell code in-memory using the System.Management.Automation API, establishes an outbound encrypted connection to a remote C2 server, receives attacker commands, executes them on the victim system, and exfiltrates the results, enabling persistent covert remote access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Executing PowerShell code in-memory via a .NET application is a sophisticated evasion technique that bypasses security controls monitoring powershell.exe or on-disk scripts. The use of encrypted C2 communication for remote command execution and data exfiltration is a hallmark of advanced backdoor malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate .NET applications do not typically execute arbitrary PowerShell code in-memory, nor do they establish persistent encrypted C2 channels to receive and execute remote commands or exfiltrate data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate administrative or automation tools may use in-memory PowerShell execution for local automation tasks, but not for persistent, covert remote access or C2-driven command execution.
key_indicators: In-memory PowerShell execution via System.Management.Automation in .NET
No powershell.exe process spawned despite PowerShell activity
Persistent outbound encrypted connections to external C2 infrastructure
Dynamic loading and execution of attacker-supplied PowerShell commands

attack_chain.action: Initial infection occurs via phishing email or exploitation, delivering the malicious .NET executable containing the PowerLess Backdoor to the victim system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the malicious .NET payload on the victim system

attack_chain.action: The malicious .NET application is executed, which loads and runs PowerShell code in-memory using the System.Management.Automation API, without launching powershell.exe or writing scripts to disk.
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishment of an encrypted communication channel with the attacker's C2 server

attack_chain.action: The implant receives attacker-supplied commands from the C2 server, executes them in-memory, and exfiltrates the results and collected data back to the C2 server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent covert remote access and can exfiltrate sensitive data from the victim system

behavioral_signatures: In-memory PowerShell execution from a .NET process using System.Management.Automation
Absence of powershell.exe process despite observable PowerShell activity
Persistent outbound encrypted network connections from .NET processes to external IPs/domains
Dynamic loading and execution of PowerShell code within .NET applications
Unusual child process creation or lack thereof in .NET applications performing system-level actions
file_indicators: Unknown or suspicious .NET executables located in user profile or temporary directories
No corresponding PowerShell script files on disk despite PowerShell activity
Presence of .NET executables with obfuscated or non-standard filenames
network_indicators: Outbound encrypted connections from .NET processes to attacker-controlled C2 domains or IP addresses
C2 traffic using uncommon ports or protocols for .NET applications
Obfuscated or non-standard HTTP/S traffic patterns originating from .NET executables
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for .NET processes that load and execute PowerShell code in-memory using the System.Management.Automation namespace without spawning powershell.exe. Correlate with persistent outbound encrypted network connections to known or suspected C2 infrastructure. Flag unknown .NET executables in user or temp directories, especially those lacking corresponding on-disk PowerShell scripts. Use EDR solutions capable of detecting in-memory script execution, anomalous process behaviors, and suspicious network activity from non-standard applications.
